pinterest.title: Ukrainian Wedding Traditions: The Rushnyk, Vinok and Korovai Families Keep
pinterest.description: A gentle guide to Ukrainian wedding traditions, in the order they traditionally unfold: matchmaking, the joining of hands, the vinok, the korovai, the playful vykup, the parents' blessing and the church rite. Learn what the encyclopaedia records and what families often tell, and how Ukrainian-Australian and mixed-heritage couples bring these customs to a wedding in Australia.

pinterest.title: What Is a Korovai? The Ukrainian Wedding Bread Shared With Every Guest
pinterest.description: The korovai is a traditional braided wedding bread of wheat flour, decorated with little dough figures of the sun, moon, birds and animals. Traditionally it was baked to wedding songs, used to bless the couple before the ceremony and shared with every guest afterwards. Ideas for giving the korovai a place at your reception.

pinterest.title: The Vinok: How the Ukrainian Bridal Wreath Was Traditionally Made
pinterest.description: In Ukrainian wedding traditions, the wreaths (vinky) were ritually made using periwinkle, a plant that plays an important role in Ukrainian folklore and wedding rituals. Ribbons, flowers and the order of the weaving vary from family to family. A practical tip: ask your florist early whether periwinkle is in season where you marry.

slides: Ukrainian wedding traditions you might not know, in the order they traditionally unfold
The rushnyk: a long embroidered cloth traditionally used in folk rites, particularly for weddings. If your family has one, it is the most portable heirloom you can bring to the day.
Zaruchyny, the betrothal, was symbolised by the joining of hands. Today it can be a family dinner where you join hands before both sets of parents.
The vinok: wreaths were ritually made using periwinkle. Ribbons, flowers and the order of the weaving vary from family to family.
The korovai: a braided wedding bread decorated with dough figures of the sun, moon, birds and animals, traditionally shared with every guest.
The vykup: a playful game at the bride's door. Keep it short, keep it kind.
The parents' blessing: one of the customs still preserved today, if in simpler form. For many families it is the emotional centre of the morning.
Which customs matter most to your family? Tell us in the comments, or talk it through with a Wedded Advisor. Link in bio.
instagram_carousel.caption:
If one of you grew up with a grandmother's embroidered towel folded in the linen cupboard, you already know Ukrainian wedding traditions are more than a list of curiosities.

Traditionally, the Ukrainian wedding was a sequence: a visit from the matchmakers, a joining of hands, a wreath, a loaf, a game at the door, a blessing, a church rite, then a long evening of song.

Many of the old rituals are no longer practised, and those that survive, such as the blessing and the wedding bread, are considerably simplified. So treat them as a menu your family chooses from, not a script every household follows. Some details, like the bread and salt welcome or who steps onto the rushnyk first, are family stories rather than recorded rites, so ask your own family what theirs mean to them.

For the church rite, start with your parish priest. Ukrainian Catholic and Orthodox parishes may differ, and your priest has the final word on how a family rushnyk may be used.

Choose the two or three customs that matter most, write them down early, and build the day around them. When you are ready, a Wedded Advisor can talk through how those moments fit the celebration you have in mind.

Read the full guide via the link in our bio.

newsletter.preview: The rushnyk, the vinok, the korovai and the parents' blessing, and how to bring them to your day.
newsletter.blurb: Some of the most meaningful wedding moments are the ones a parent or grandparent quietly asks for. Our new guide to Ukrainian wedding traditions walks through the customs in the order they traditionally unfold: the rushnyk, the vinok, the korovai shared with every guest, the playful vykup at the bride's door and the parents' blessing. It separates what is recorded from what families often tell, and shows how Ukrainian-Australian and mixed-heritage couples bring these customs to a wedding in Australia.
